role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Bottom line first: the answer before the reasons
summary: People decide on the first thing they hear and remember the last. This lesson teaches bottom line up front, the pyramid principle and the rule of three, so that a busy lender, partner or contractor gets your answer in one sentence and your reasons in three.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the person across the table is deciding from your first sentence, so make your first sentence the answer. Reasons come second, evidence third, and nothing comes first that the listener has to wait through to find out what you want.

Recall

Q. Does tiredness excuse a signature or an emailed approval?

A. No. In general a commitment binds you however tired you were when you made it, which is why the red window keeps signatures and approvals out of your worst hours.

Q. What is the first question to ask about any adviser's recommendation?

A. How is this person paid, and what does the recommendation do to their pay? Incentives explain behaviour before character does.

Q. What does a go/no-go gate need before you arrive at it?

A. Written criteria, agreed in advance, so the decision at the gate is a comparison against the criteria and not a mood on the day.

Why this matters

A developer sells all the time. You sell the deal to a lender, the design to a planning officer, the schedule to a contractor and the risk to a partner. Every one of those people is busy, and most of them are deciding whether to keep listening within the first minute. If your answer arrives in minute four, after the history, the context and the caveats, many of them have already filed you under "unclear" and moved on. Clarity is not a soft skill here. It decides how fast you get a yes, and time on a development project is money: interest, rent on land you cannot use, and a team you are paying to wait.

Bottom line up front

In plain English: say the conclusion first. If you want a decision, say the decision you want. If you are reporting a problem, say the problem and what you recommend before you explain how it happened.

The professional framing is a military one, and you will recognise it. Bottom line up front, usually shortened to BLUF, is a writing and briefing standard used across armed forces: the first line of a message states the conclusion, the request or the decision required. The reader can stop after one line and still act correctly. Everything after that line is support.

Worked example one. Here is a hypothetical update to a lender, written the usual way: "Following the site meeting on Tuesday, where the structural engineer reviewed the test pits, and after discussion with the contractor about sequencing, we have considered several options for the foundation, and on balance..." By the time the lender reaches the request, the request is buried. The BLUF version: "We are asking you to approve a 3-week schedule extension at no change to the loan amount. The cause is a foundation redesign after test pits found softer soil than expected. The cost is absorbed by contingency. Details below." Same facts. The lender can say yes after reading two lines.

The pyramid: one answer, three supports

Plain English: an argument is a pyramid. The answer sits on top. Under it sit a small number of reasons, ideally three. Under each reason sits its evidence. You deliver it top down.

The professional framing is the pyramid principle, developed by Barbara Minto at McKinsey and set out in her book The Pyramid Principle. Two disciplines make it work. First, every level summarises the level below it, so if someone asks "why?" of the answer, the three reasons are the reply, and if they ask "why?" of a reason, its evidence is the reply. Second, the reasons at one level should not overlap and should together cover the case. Consultants call that being mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. You do not need the jargon. You need the habit of checking that your three reasons are three different things, and that nothing important is missing.

Worked example two. Suppose, as a hypothetical, you are recommending to a partner that you walk away from a site. Top of the pyramid: "We should not buy this site at the asking price." Three supports. One, the price implies rents about 15 percent above anything achieved nearby. Two, the soil report flags a possible need for deep foundations, which the price does not allow for. Three, the seller will not grant a conditional period long enough to test either point. Each support then has its evidence: the rent comparables, the geotechnical memo and the draft agreement. If the partner pushes back, you go down one level, to the specific point they doubt, and nowhere else.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: answer first, three reasons, evidence on request.

Why three, and when to pause

The rule of three is a practitioner habit with some support in research on working memory: people hold a small number of items in mind at once, and lists of three are easy to follow and to repeat. Treat the exact number as a guide, not a law. Two reasons can feel thin; five usually means two of them are the same point or one of them is weak. A weak fourth reason does damage, because a sceptical listener attacks the weakest point and then treats the whole case as weak.

Pace and pause matter as much as order. After you state the bottom line, stop for a breath. That pause tells the listener the important sentence has just been said, and it gives them a moment to react. Many people rush the answer and slow down for the background, which is exactly backwards. While we are on delivery, one correction. You may have heard that 93 percent of communication is non-verbal. That figure comes from narrow experiments by the psychologist Albert Mehrabian on how people judged feelings when tone and a single word disagreed. It was never a finding about how people understand an argument. Your words carry your case. Tone and pace decide whether people trust you while you make it.

How the best do it

Large contractors and owners running big programmes tend to standardise the top of every report. A typical monthly owner's report opens with a one-page dashboard: status against budget and schedule, the top risks, and the decisions needed from the owner, with dates. The detail follows in sections the reader can skip. A small developer can copy this for free. Open every report, email and meeting with the same three lines: where we are, what is at risk, what I need from you and by when.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a request that is never clearly made. The listener nods, the meeting ends warmly, and nobody has agreed to anything. Weeks later you discover the lender thought you were giving an update, not asking for approval. The control is to write your bottom line as a single sentence before any meeting or message, and to make it a request with a date where a decision is needed: "I am asking you to approve X by Friday." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to send the message.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tells the story in the order it happened, because that is the order he lived it. Chronology feels honest and thorough. To the listener it is a puzzle with the answer hidden at the end. The second mistake is hedging the bottom line until it means nothing: "We may possibly want to consider looking at an extension." Hedge in the evidence, where uncertainty belongs, not in the request.

Callback

In Week 1 you learned the gate meeting: a planned point where the next block of money is either committed or not, against written criteria. A gate meeting is where bottom line first earns its keep. Open with the recommendation, go or no-go, then the three criteria and how the project stands against each. If the decision makers have to hunt for your recommendation, the gate turns into a discussion, and discussions drift past dates.

Recap

Lead with the answer. Support it with about three reasons that do not overlap and together cover the case. Hold evidence in reserve for whoever asks. Pause after the bottom line, and keep the request specific and dated. Words carry the case; delivery decides whether you are trusted while you make it.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and the warning that was buried on a slide.
checklist: Write the bottom line of your next important message as one sentence before writing anything else.
Turn every request into a request with a date: what you want approved and by when.
List no more than three reasons, and check that no two of them are the same point.
Keep evidence in reserve and go down one level only to the point that is challenged.
Open every report with where we are, what is at risk and what I need from you.
Pause for a breath after you say the bottom line aloud.
Move hedging out of the request and into the evidence, where uncertainty belongs.
head: Field checklist
speak: The person I am talking to is deciding from my first sentence, so my first sentence is the answer. That is bottom line up front, the standard most militaries use for messages: the reader can stop after one line and still act correctly. Behind the answer I give about three reasons, and I check that each one is a different point and that together they cover the case. Behind each reason I hold the evidence, and I only go down to it when someone challenges that specific reason. That is the pyramid principle. After I say the bottom line, I pause, so the listener knows the important sentence has been said. If I need a decision, I make the request specific and dated: I am asking you to approve this by Friday. If I cannot write that one sentence before a meeting, I am not ready for the meeting. And I do not tell the story in the order it happened. Chronology hides the answer at the end.
terms: Bottom line up front (BLUF) — a message standard in which the first line states the conclusion, request or decision required.
Pyramid principle — structuring an argument as one answer on top, a few supporting reasons beneath it, and evidence beneath each reason.
Rule of three — the practitioner habit of grouping key points in threes because listeners follow and remember them easily.

hostile.q: You have talked for five minutes. What exactly are you asking me for?
hostile.a: I am asking you to approve a 3-week schedule extension at no change to the loan amount, by Friday. The cause is a foundation redesign, and contingency covers the cost. I should have opened with that, and I can take you through any of the three points behind it.

title: Columbia: the warning that was buried on a slide
summary: The space shuttle Columbia was lost in 2003 after a foam strike at launch damaged its wing. Engineers raised concerns, but the decisive uncertainty reached decision makers buried under a reassuring headline. This lesson takes the case through seven steps and ends with Rule 5.
rule: Rule 5: When a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out; I never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question.
body:
Columbia was not lost for want of a concern. Engineers had one, and they said it. It was lost, in part, because the concern travelled upward in a form that let the people at the top read reassurance where the evidence said uncertainty.

Recall

Q. What does bottom line up front require of a message?

A. The first line states the conclusion, request or decision required, so the reader can stop after one line and still act correctly.

Q. What is Rule 3?

A. When a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.

Q. What is a reference class, in one sentence?

A. A group of similar past cases whose actual outcomes give you a base rate to start from before you adjust for what is different about yours.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a development project runs on reports passed upward: a geotechnical memo to the engineer, the engineer's note to the project manager, the project manager's summary to you, your summary to the lender. Every hand-off compresses. If the compression strips out the uncertainty, the person with the authority to spend money on finding out never learns that finding out was needed. That is the mechanism of this case, and it is a communication failure as much as a technical one. Read the investigation report itself before you quote any detail; what follows is the shape of its findings.

Step 1: Timeline

Columbia launched in January 2003. During ascent, a piece of insulating foam broke away from the external fuel tank and struck the leading edge of the left wing. The strike was seen on launch film the next day. Engineers formed a team to assess the debris strike while the crew carried on with a mission of about two weeks. On 1 February 2003, during re-entry, hot gas entered the damaged wing and the orbiter broke apart. All seven crew members died. The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reported later that year. It found the physical cause in the wing damage, and it gave equal weight to organisational causes, including how risk was communicated.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. First, the debris team's analysis relied on a model that had been built and tested for pieces of debris far smaller than the one seen on film, and that limitation was not carried forward prominently. Second, requests from engineers for imagery of the wing in orbit were not pursued to a conclusion; the investigation found that the management chain treated the question as settled before it was. Third, the mission's managers accepted a summary that the strike was not a safety-of-flight issue, and the mission continued on that basis.

Step 3: Assumptions

The governing assumption was that foam strikes were a known maintenance problem, not a flight safety risk. Foam had come off on earlier flights without loss, and each survival made the next strike look more normal. The investigation borrowed a term from the sociologist Diane Vaughan for this: normalisation of deviance, where a departure from the design intent is repeated, nothing bad happens, and the departure quietly becomes the new standard. The second assumption was that the analysis tool fitted the case. It did not, because the piece of foam was hundreds of times larger than the cases it had been calibrated on.

Step 4: Incentives

The schedule pressed on everyone. The programme had a demanding launch timetable, and a finding that foam was a flight safety issue would have grounded the fleet. Nobody needed to be dishonest for that pressure to work. It is enough that the answer "this is fine" is cheap and fast, and the answer "we do not know" is expensive and slow. The cultural incentive mattered too: the investigation found that engineers felt the burden was on them to prove the vehicle unsafe, rather than on managers to show it was safe.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

This is where communication sits at the centre. One briefing slide from the debris assessment is now taught in courses on information design, and the investigation board drew on the analysis of the designer Edward Tufte. The slide's headline said, in substance, that review of test data indicated conservatism, meaning the test results suggested the tiles could take more than the model predicted. Lower down, in small type and under several levels of bullets, sat the decisive fact: the piece that hit Columbia was vastly larger than the test pieces, so the test data did not cover the case. The reassurance was on top. The open question was at the bottom. A reader skimming the headline would conclude the opposite of what the evidence actually supported.

The second warning sign was the imagery requests. Several engineers asked, through more than one route, for the wing to be photographed. The requests stalled partly because they did not arrive through the channel managers expected, and partly because nobody stated plainly what the images might change.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: the headline said safe, the footnote said unknown, and people read the headline.

Step 6: Point of no return

The physical point of no return was launch, when the damage was done. The decision point of no return came earlier in the mission than re-entry: the investigation considered whether a rescue or a repair could have been attempted, and found that options existed in principle but needed the damage to be recognised early, while there was still time to act. Every day spent treating the question as closed used up that time. The lesson for a developer is that a recoverable problem has a window, and unclear communication spends the window.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was an organisation that had come to accept a known anomaly as normal, and a reporting style that let uncertainty sink beneath reassurance. The technical and the communication causes are joined. If the first line of that slide had read, "We cannot rule out serious wing damage; our model does not cover a piece this size; imagery would tell us," the decision at the top would at least have been made with the right question in front of it.

The prevention rule

Rule 5: When a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out; I never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question.

Worked example one, applied. A geotechnical engineer sends you a hypothetical memo that opens, "Bearing capacity appears adequate for the proposed footings." On page three: "Two of six boreholes encountered soft clay; extent not determined." The Rule 5 rewrite for your lender update: "Foundation risk is open. Two of six boreholes found soft clay. Four more boreholes, about 2 weeks and a modest fee, would tell us whether footings still work." That sentence costs you nothing and buys you a decision made with the facts in view.

Worked example two. Your contractor's weekly report reads "Schedule on track" at the top, and lists at the bottom "steel shop drawings outstanding, fabricator lead time 10 weeks." If steel is needed in 8 weeks, the report is reassuring and wrong. Rewrite: "Steel is at risk: shop drawings are late and fabrication takes 10 weeks against 8 available. Decision needed this week on approving drawings in two parts."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk on your own projects is the reassuring summary of an uncertain report. The control is a habit and a question. The habit: read the last page of every technical report first, where limitations and exclusions live. The question, asked of every summary handed to you: "What does this not cover, and what would it take to find out?"

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a risk he does not want as a risk that is small. He reads "appears adequate" as "adequate". Hedged words in a technical report are usually deliberate; they are the writer telling you where the evidence stops.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the outside view: start from what actually happened to similar cases. Columbia shows its shadow. Each earlier flight that survived a foam strike became the reference class that made the next strike look safe. A reference class built from your own near-misses is not evidence of safety. It is a count of times you were lucky.

Recap

Columbia's foam strike was seen, analysed and discussed. What failed was the path from the analysis to the decision: a tool used outside its range, a headline that reassured above a footnote that warned, and requests for evidence that stalled. Rule 5 puts the risk in the first line, with what it would take to close it.

Next: JAX, The Money, on how a clear ask shortens the time to a yes, and what that time is worth.
checklist: Read the limitations and exclusions page of every technical report before its summary.
Ask of every summary: what does this not cover, and what would it take to find out?
Put any open risk in the first line of your own updates, in plain words.
State what evidence would close the risk, its rough cost and its time.
Treat hedged words such as appears, generally and not determined as deliberate signals.
Never let repeated survival of a known problem stand in for proof that it is safe.
Name one person responsible for chasing each request for evidence to an answer.
head: Field checklist
speak: Columbia was lost in 2003 after foam from the fuel tank struck the left wing during launch. The strike was seen and analysed while the crew was in orbit. What failed was the path from the evidence to the decision. The analysis tool had been calibrated on pieces of debris far smaller than the one that hit, and that fact sat in small type at the bottom of a briefing slide whose headline suggested the tiles had margin. Engineers asked for photographs of the wing, and the requests stalled. Earlier flights had survived foam strikes, so the problem had come to feel normal. My rule, Rule 5: when a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out. I never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question. On my projects that means reading the limitations page of every report first.
terms: Normalisation of deviance — the process by which a repeated departure from the design intent, survived without loss, comes to be treated as acceptable.
Safety of flight — in aviation and spaceflight, a condition that could endanger the vehicle or crew, as opposed to a maintenance matter.
Limitations section — the part of a technical report that states what the analysis does not cover and where its evidence stops.

hostile.q: Your geotechnical summary says bearing capacity is adequate. Why should I believe there is no foundation risk?
hostile.a: You should not take it as no risk. Two of six boreholes found soft clay and the extent is not yet known. Four more boreholes, about two weeks and a modest fee, would close the question, and I have authorised them. Until they report, I am carrying the foundation as an open risk with contingency against it.

title: What a clear ask is worth: the price of a slow yes
summary: On a development project every week of waiting costs interest, overhead and risk, and an unclear request adds weeks. This lesson prices decision delay, shows how a vague ask turns into a second and third round of questions, and sets out the one-page ask that gets a yes on the first read.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an unclear request does not fail loudly. It fails by coming back with questions, and every round of questions costs a week, and every week on a funded project has a price you can calculate.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 5 say?

A. When a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out; never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question.

Q. In Week 4, how did Petra plan a sharp two o'clock meeting after night shifts?

A. She worked backward from the meeting time to set sleep, light and caffeine, so the decision landed in a good hour rather than wherever the shift left it.

Q. What is profit on cost?

A. Development profit divided by total development cost, a quick measure of how much margin the project carries against what it costs to build.

Why this matters

Most of your projects will run on borrowed money, and borrowed money charges by the day. Many approvals you need, from a lender, a partner, a planning officer or a contractor, sit on the critical path, which means nothing else can move until they arrive. If your request is clear, the approval comes in one round. If it is vague, it comes back with questions, you answer, they ask again, and two or three weeks pass. You will rarely see that cost on a report, because no one invoices you for it. That is exactly why you need to be able to price it yourself.

The meter is always running

In plain English: once you have bought land or drawn a loan, the project costs money every week whether or not anything happens. Interest accrues. Your own overhead, the team, the insurance and the site security keep running. That weekly figure is the carrying cost.

The professional framing is cost of delay: the value lost per unit of time that a decision or task on the critical path is late. Lenders, cost managers and schedulers all use it, in different words. For a developer the core of it is interest plus fixed overhead, and on top of that there is a less visible cost: the market can move while you wait.

Worked example one. Suppose, as a hypothetical, you have drawn 6,000,000 dollars of a construction loan at 8 percent interest a year. Annual interest is 6,000,000 times 0.08, which equals 480,000 dollars. Divide by 52 weeks: about 9,230 dollars a week. Add hypothetical fixed overhead of 5,000 dollars a week for your team, insurance and site costs. The carrying cost is about 14,230 dollars a week. Call it 14,000 dollars. Now suppose a vague request to the lender costs two extra rounds of questions at one week each. That is about 28,000 dollars of cost created by the way the email was written. If the delay also pushes the contractor's crew off the job and they charge a remobilisation fee, the figure grows.

Why vague requests come back

Plain English: a reader who cannot find the request, cannot tell what it costs, or cannot see what happens if they say no will ask. Each of those questions is a round.

The professional framing comes from how credit and investment committees work. An analyst or account manager takes your request to a committee. If your message does not let them answer the committee's standard questions, which are what is being asked, why, what it costs, what the risk is and what the alternative is, the analyst sends the questions back to you. You are not writing to the person who reads your email. You are writing to the meeting that person has to brief.

Worked example two, the one-page ask. Here is a hypothetical request for a partner to fund a cost increase, written to be approved in one round. "Request: approve an additional 400,000 dollars of equity by 15 March. Why: the contractor's revised price for the parking structure came in 400,000 dollars over budget after redesign. Effect on returns: projected profit falls from 3,000,000 to 2,600,000 dollars, profit on cost from about 15 percent to about 13 percent. Alternative considered: cutting 20 parking spaces saves about 300,000 dollars but breaches the parking condition in the planning approval. Risk if we wait: the contractor's price holds until 20 March. Recommendation: approve." Every committee question is answered before it is asked.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: request, why, effect on returns, alternative, risk of waiting, recommendation.

The return you lose to the calendar

Delay does more than add cost. It stretches time, and investors measure returns over time. The internal rate of return, or IRR, which you will meet properly in Week 15, is roughly the annual rate the investment earns; it falls when the same profit takes longer to arrive. You do not need the formula today. You need the direction: a delay costs you twice, once in carry that reduces profit, and again because the reduced profit arrives later.

A simple illustration, without the IRR formula. Suppose a hypothetical project returns 2,600,000 dollars of profit on 4,000,000 dollars of equity over 24 months. That is a profit of 65 percent over two years. Stretch it to 26 months with the 28,000 dollars of carry above, and profit is 2,572,000 dollars over 26 months. The total barely moves, but the yearly return falls by more than you might expect, because the same money took two more months. On a rough simple annual basis, ignoring compounding, 65 percent over 24 months is about 32.5 percent a year. Then 2,572,000 dollars on 4,000,000 is about 64.3 percent, and over 26 months that is about 29.7 percent a year. Profit fell by about 1 percent. The yearly return fell by nearly 3 percentage points. That gap is the calendar charging you, and it is why investors care about speed as much as about cost. Partners notice that, and a sponsor with a reputation for slow decisions pays for it in the terms on the next deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not one slow email. It is a pattern of them, which a lender or partner learns to read as a sponsor who does not know what he wants. That reputation shows up later as tighter conditions, more reporting and a higher price for money. The control is the six-line ask above, used for every decision request, and a rule that no request leaves your desk without a date and a stated consequence of waiting. Then keep score. For a month, note how many rounds each request takes before it is approved. Any request that needed more than one round is a draft you can learn from: find the question that came back, and add its answer to your template.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a longer, more detailed email shows diligence. It usually shows the opposite: that the writer has not decided what matters. The second mistake is asking for approval without stating the alternative. A committee that cannot see what you rejected will ask you to go back and consider options, which is another round.

Callback

In Week 1, Sage showed you where the money sits at each stage of a project, and how much is committed before anything is built. The more money committed, the higher the carrying cost each week, so clarity matters most late in a project, exactly when everyone is busiest and most tempted to send a hurried, half-formed request. The weeks when the meter runs fastest are the weeks your asks must be cleanest.

Recap

Carrying cost is interest plus fixed overhead, per week, and it runs whether or not anything happens. Vague requests come back as rounds of questions, and each round costs a week. Write to the committee, not to the reader: request, why, effect on returns, alternative, risk of waiting, recommendation. Delay hurts twice, through lower profit and later profit. All figures in this lesson are hypothetical.

Next: LEX, The Rules, on when what you say or write binds you: emails, notices and the words "subject to contract".
checklist: Calculate your project's weekly carrying cost: interest plus fixed overhead.
Before sending any request, check it answers: what, why, cost, alternative, risk of waiting.
Put a date and a stated consequence of waiting on every decision request.
State the effect on profit and on profit on cost for any cost change you ask a partner to fund.
Name the alternative you considered and why you rejected it.
Write for the committee your reader must brief, not only for the reader.
Track how many rounds each of your requests takes, and fix the ones that need more than one.
head: Field checklist
speak: Once I own land or have drawn a loan, my project costs money every week whether or not anything happens. Interest plus fixed overhead is my carrying cost, and I can calculate it. On a hypothetical 6 million dollar loan at 8 percent, interest alone is about 9,000 dollars a week. An unclear request to a lender or partner rarely gets a no. It gets questions, and each round of questions costs a week. So I write every request to answer the committee's standard questions before they are asked: what I am asking for, why, the effect on returns, the alternative I rejected, the risk of waiting, and my recommendation, with a date. Delay costs me twice: carry reduces the profit, and the profit arrives later, which lowers the annual return. A pattern of vague asks also costs me reputation, which a lender prices into the next deal.
terms: Carrying cost — the cost a project incurs per unit of time, mainly interest and fixed overhead, whether or not work progresses.
Cost of delay — the value lost for each unit of time a decision or task on the critical path is late.
Critical path — the chain of dependent tasks that sets the earliest finish date, so any delay on it delays the whole project.

hostile.q: Why should I approve 400,000 dollars more equity this week instead of taking a month to think about it?
hostile.a: Because waiting has a price. The contractor's revised price holds until 20 March, and our carrying cost is about 14,000 dollars a week. I have considered the alternative of cutting parking, which breaches a planning condition. Profit falls from 3 million to 2.6 million on these hypothetical figures, and that is the best remaining option. I am asking for a decision by 15 March.

title: When your words bind: emails, notices and “subject to contract”
summary: Clear communication has a legal edge: a clear email can form or change an agreement, and a notice sent the wrong way can be no notice at all. This lesson explains how words become commitments, what notice clauses require, and what labels such as subject to contract and without prejudice are meant to do.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the clearer you write, the more your words can be held against you as a promise. That is not a reason to write vaguely. It is a reason to decide, before you hit send, whether you mean to commit, and to say so.

Recall

Q. In the two o'clock meeting, what is the first thing you do when a hard question lands?

A. Pause and breathe before answering, so your state is steady and the answer is chosen rather than reflexive.

Q. What is your walk-away price?

A. The worst terms you will accept, decided from your own analysis before the negotiation, so the other side's anchor cannot move it.

Q. Who holds the gate at the certificate of occupancy?

A. The authority having jurisdiction, through its building official, which decides whether the completed building may be lawfully occupied.

Why this matters

Most of a developer's business is done by email, message and phone. Prices are agreed, scope is changed and deadlines are extended in a few lines typed between meetings. Courts in many countries have been willing to find that a binding agreement, or a binding change to one, was made through exactly that kind of exchange. Meanwhile the formal contract may say that some things, such as a notice of default or a claim for extra time, only count if they are sent in a specific way. Good communication on a project therefore has two halves: saying clearly what you mean, and knowing which of your words the law, or the contract, will treat as binding. This lesson teaches concepts only. Whether a particular exchange binds you depends on the law that applies and on the documents; that needs a lawyer.

How words become commitments

Plain English: in most common-law systems, a contract needs an offer, an acceptance of that offer, something of value exchanged, and an intention to be legally bound. Writing and signatures are often not required at all, though some kinds of contract, commonly including contracts for the sale of land, may need to be in writing under statute. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The professional framing is that courts usually judge intention objectively. They ask what a reasonable person, reading the exchange, would conclude the parties meant, not what one party privately intended. So an email that reads like an acceptance can be treated as one, even if you meant it as a step in a negotiation.

Worked example one. Suppose, as a hypothetical, a contractor emails: "We can do the extra excavation for 85,000 dollars, starting Monday. Please confirm." You reply from your phone: "Fine, go ahead." The contractor starts. You later discover the work was already in the original scope. Depending on the contract and the law that applies, you may have agreed a change at that price, and arguing it was a misunderstanding is much harder after the work is done. The clear alternative: "Do not start. I believe this is in the original scope under the excavation item. Please show me why it is extra, and we will agree a price before any work."

Labels that try to stop a commitment

Plain English: parties often put words on their correspondence to signal that it is not yet binding. Two of the most common are "subject to contract" and "without prejudice".

"Subject to contract" is a label used in many common-law places to signal that no binding agreement exists until a formal document is signed. It is often effective, but it is not a magic spell. If the parties then behave as though the deal is done, for example by starting work or paying money, a court may find that they waived the label or made a contract by conduct. "Without prejudice" is different. It is generally used to protect genuine attempts to settle a dispute, so that an offer made to resolve a disagreement cannot later be shown to a court as an admission. It usually only works where there is a real dispute and a real attempt to settle it; writing it on an ordinary business email does little. Rules vary by jurisdiction. Verify against the primary source and with your lawyer before you rely on either label.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: labels help, but conduct can override them, so I act the way I want the deal read.

Notices: the right words sent the wrong way

Plain English: formal contracts, such as construction contracts, loan agreements and leases, usually contain a notices clause. It says how official notices must be given: in writing, to a named person, at a stated address, by stated methods, and when they are treated as received. Many construction contracts also require notice of a claim for extra time or money within a set period after the event.

The professional framing is that these clauses are often enforced strictly. A notice sent by text message when the contract requires a letter or a specified email address, or sent to the site manager when it must go to the company's registered office, may not count. A claim notice sent late may lose the claim, depending on the wording and the law. The deadline in your contract is a contract term, not a standard; read the actual clause.

Worked example two. Suppose a hypothetical loan agreement says a borrower must notify the lender of any event that could delay completion "in writing to the agent at the address in Schedule 1, within 10 business days." On day 3 of a delay you mention it on a call with the lender's relationship manager. On day 14 the agent says no notice was received. You told the right organisation, but not the right person, not in the required form and not in time. The control is a notice register: for every major contract, one line listing what must be noticed, how, to whom, by when, and the date you sent it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the casual yes: a short reply, sent quickly, that the other side reasonably treats as agreement to a price, a scope or a deadline. The control is a sentence you train into your fingers. When you are not agreeing, say so: "This is not an approval. We will confirm in writing once the price is agreed." When you are agreeing, say exactly what: the scope, the price and any conditions. Ambiguity helps whoever is better at arguing later. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the jurisdiction that governs the contract, for any notice of default, claim or termination.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks that because nothing was signed, nothing was agreed. The second mistake is the reverse: sending formal notices by whatever channel is fastest, because the other side "obviously knows". Knowing is not the test. The contract's notice clause is.

Callback

In Week 3 you met misrepresentation: a false statement of fact that induces someone to enter a contract can give them remedies, whatever the entire-agreement clause says. This week adds the other side of the same coin. Statements can create liability if they are false, and replies can create obligations if they read as agreement. Every message you send is either a fact you must be able to stand behind or a commitment you must mean.

Recap

Agreement is usually judged objectively, so a clear reply can bind you. Labels such as subject to contract and without prejudice have specific purposes and limits, and conduct can override them. Notices must follow the contract's clause on form, recipient and timing. Say when you are not agreeing, say exactly what you are agreeing to when you are, and keep a notice register. Verify every point against the law that applies and with a lawyer.

Next: Sage, The Numbers, building a three-line summary from a simple hypothetical deal and saying it aloud.
checklist: Decide before you send whether a message is meant to commit you, and say which.
Use a standard non-approval line when you are not agreeing to a price or scope.
When you agree, state the exact scope, price and conditions in the reply.
Read the notices clause of every major contract and record its form, recipient and timing.
Keep a notice register: what must be noticed, how, to whom, by when, date sent.
Do not start or pay for work under a subject to contract deal unless you mean it to bind.
Send any notice of default, claim or termination only after a lawyer has reviewed it.
head: Field checklist
speak: In most common-law systems, a contract needs an offer, an acceptance, something of value and an intention to be bound, and courts judge intention by what a reasonable person would read in the exchange, not by what I privately meant. So a quick reply like fine, go ahead can be treated as agreement to a price or a scope change. When I am not agreeing, I say so in writing. When I am, I state exactly what. Labels such as subject to contract can signal that nothing binds yet, but if we start work or pay money, a court may find a deal by conduct. Without prejudice is meant to protect real settlement talks, not ordinary emails. Formal contracts also have notice clauses, and a notice sent the wrong way, to the wrong person or too late may not count. So I keep a notice register, and a lawyer reviews any notice of default or claim. All of this varies by jurisdiction.
terms: Notices clause — a contract term that sets how formal notices must be given, to whom, by what method and when they count as received.
Subject to contract — a label signalling that negotiations are not yet binding until a formal agreement is signed, which conduct can override.
Without prejudice — a label generally used to protect genuine attempts to settle a dispute from being used later as admissions.

hostile.q: You told us about the delay on a call two weeks ago. Why should we accept that as notice?
hostile.a: I should have sent it in the form the agreement requires, and I am sending a formal notice to the agent today. I will also confirm in writing the date of our call and what was said. Going forward, every notifiable event goes on my notice register and is sent in the required form, to the named recipient, within the period.

title: Three numbers and a bottom line: building the summary from the arithmetic
summary: A bottom line you can defend is built from arithmetic you have done yourself. This lesson works a simple hypothetical rental project from rent to value to profit, picks the three numbers the result depends on, tests one of them, and fits the whole summary into a two-minute spoken slot.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the bottom line is the last thing you calculate and the first thing you say. Do the arithmetic forward, find the three numbers it hangs on, and then write one sentence that a listener can repeat to someone else.

Recall

Q. You take 200 milligrams of caffeine ten hours before bed, with a planning half-life of five hours. How much remains?

A. Ten hours is two half-lives, so one quarter remains, about 50 milligrams.

Q. Does an entire-agreement clause protect a seller who made a false statement of fact?

A. Often not fully. In many systems a misrepresentation that induced the contract can still give remedies, depending on the wording and the law; verify with a lawyer.

Q. How do you decide whether a study is worth paying for?

A. Compare its cost with the expected value of the better decision it allows, which is the chance it changes your decision times what that change is worth.

Why this matters

Every pitch to a lender or partner ends in one sentence about value. If you cannot rebuild that sentence from its parts on a whiteboard, the first good question will expose you. If you can, you are not reciting a number someone handed you; you own it. This lesson uses three terms you will study in depth in Phase 2: net operating income, cap rate and profit on cost. Today they are only tools for building a bottom line, defined as we go. All figures are hypothetical and round.

Step 1: From rent to income

Take a hypothetical new building of 40 apartments, each renting for 2,000 dollars a month.

Potential rent: 40 apartments times 2,000 dollars times 12 months equals 960,000 dollars a year. This is the rent if every unit is let all year.

Vacancy: some units will be empty between tenants. Assume 5 percent. 960,000 times 0.05 equals 48,000 dollars. Effective income: 960,000 minus 48,000 equals 912,000 dollars a year.

Operating expenses: taxes, insurance, repairs, management and utilities the landlord pays. Assume 35 percent of effective income. 912,000 times 0.35 equals 319,200 dollars.

Net operating income, or NOI, is income after operating expenses and before loan payments and income tax: 912,000 minus 319,200 equals 592,800 dollars a year.

Step 2: From income to value to profit

A capitalisation rate, or cap rate, is the ratio buyers in a market pay between a property's NOI and its price. If buyers pay a price at which NOI is 6 percent of value, the cap rate is 6 percent. The ratio is market evidence, not a standard; it moves with interest rates and investor appetite.

Value: NOI divided by cap rate. 592,800 divided by 0.06 equals 9,880,000 dollars.

Cost: assume a hypothetical total development cost of 8,500,000 dollars, covering land, construction, fees and finance.

Profit: value minus cost. 9,880,000 minus 8,500,000 equals 1,380,000 dollars.

Profit on cost: profit divided by cost. 1,380,000 divided by 8,500,000 is about 0.162, so about 16 percent.

Step 3: Find the three numbers it hangs on

Not every input matters equally. Ask which three, if wrong, would change the answer most. Here they are rent, cap rate and total cost. Vacancy and the expense ratio matter, but less, and they move with rent in practice.

Worked example one, testing rent. Suppose rent comes in 10 percent lower, at 1,800 dollars a month. Potential rent: 40 times 1,800 times 12 equals 864,000 dollars. Vacancy at 5 percent: 43,200 dollars. Effective income: 820,800 dollars. Expenses at 35 percent: 287,280 dollars. NOI: 533,520 dollars. Value at 6 percent: 8,892,000 dollars. Profit: 8,892,000 minus 8,500,000 equals 392,000 dollars. Profit on cost: about 4.6 percent.

Read that carefully. A 10 percent fall in rent cut profit by more than 70 percent, from 1,380,000 to 392,000 dollars. That is leverage inside the arithmetic: cost stays fixed, so every dollar of lost value comes straight out of profit. A listener who hears only "16 percent" does not know that, and an honest bottom line tells them.

Run the same test on the cap rate. Suppose buyers in a year's time pay a 6.5 percent cap rate instead of 6. Value: 592,800 divided by 0.065 equals 9,120,000 dollars. Profit: 9,120,000 minus 8,500,000 equals 620,000 dollars, about 7.3 percent on cost. Half a percentage point on the cap rate took more than half the profit. So two of your three numbers are fragile, and the summary should say which is more fragile. Here it is rent, so rent goes in the sentence.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: about 1.4 million of profit on 8.5 million of cost, and most of it disappears if rent is 10 percent low.

Step 4: Write the bottom line and fit it to the clock

Now write the summary, top down, in three lines.

Line 1, the answer: "On our assumptions the project is worth about 9.9 million dollars against a cost of 8.5 million, a profit of about 1.4 million or 16 percent on cost."

Line 2, the three numbers it hangs on: "It rests on rent of 2,000 dollars a month, a 6 percent cap rate and cost of 8.5 million."

Line 3, the honest risk, Rule 5 in practice: "Rent is the sensitive one: 10 percent lower leaves profit of about 400,000 dollars, so we are testing rent before committing."

Notice the rounding. Say "about 9.9 million", not "nine million eight hundred and eighty thousand". Spoken precision beyond two significant figures sounds like rigour and lands as noise. Keep the exact figures on the page for anyone who wants them.

Worked example two, the time budget. A common practitioner estimate for conversational speech is roughly 130 to 160 words a minute; treat it as a rough guide and time yourself. Suppose you have a two-minute slot at a partner meeting and you speak at about 140 words a minute. Two minutes times 140 equals 280 words. Leave about 15 percent for pauses: 280 times 0.85 equals about 240 words. Your three lines above are about 80 words. That leaves about 160 words, roughly 50 words for each of the three numbers: where the rent comes from, what evidence supports 6 percent, and how firm the cost is. Write it, read it aloud against a timer, and cut until it fits.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a bottom line that is true on its assumptions and silent about how fragile they are. A partner who later discovers that a small change in rent wipes out most of the profit will trust none of your later numbers. The control is to run the test on your most sensitive input every time, and to say the result in the summary, not only in an appendix.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads with the inputs, because that is the order he calculated them in, and arrives at the answer just as the listener's attention runs out. The second mistake is quoting the cap rate as if it were a fact. It is an assumption about what buyers will pay, and it deserves the same scrutiny as rent.

Callback

In Week 2, Quincy worked backward from the margin you need to the estimate you can afford. Today ran the same chain forward, from rent to value to profit. Run it both ways on every deal: forward to see what the project produces, backward to see how much room you have before it stops working.

Recap

Rent minus vacancy gives effective income; minus operating expenses gives NOI; NOI divided by cap rate gives value; value minus cost gives profit. Find the three inputs the answer hangs on, test the most sensitive, and write a three-line bottom line that includes the risk. Round when you speak, keep exact figures on paper, and fit the whole thing to the clock.

Next: Kema, The Room, on listening across the table from a landowner, and what to do with silence.
checklist: Rebuild every value figure you plan to present from rent to profit yourself.
Identify the three inputs the result depends on most.
Test the most sensitive input by 10 percent and write down the effect on profit.
Write a three-line summary: the answer, the three numbers, the honest risk.
Round spoken figures to two significant figures and keep exact figures on paper.
Time yourself and fit the pitch to the slot, leaving about 15 percent for pauses.
Treat the cap rate as an assumption to be evidenced, not a fact.
head: Field checklist
speak: I build the bottom line from the arithmetic, forward. On a hypothetical 40-unit building at 2,000 dollars a month, potential rent is 960,000 dollars a year. Take 5 percent vacancy and 35 percent operating expenses and net operating income is about 593,000 dollars. Divide by a 6 percent cap rate and the building is worth about 9.9 million. Against a cost of 8.5 million, that is about 1.4 million of profit, about 16 percent on cost. The answer hangs on three numbers: rent, cap rate and cost. When I test rent 10 percent lower, profit falls to about 400,000 dollars, more than 70 percent gone, because cost stays fixed. So my summary has three lines: the answer, the three numbers, and the risk. I round when I speak, I keep the exact figures on paper, and I time the pitch so it fits the slot with room to pause.
terms: Net operating income (NOI) — a property's income after vacancy and operating expenses, before loan payments and income tax.
Capitalisation rate (cap rate) — the market ratio of a property's net operating income to its price, used to convert income into value.
Profit on cost — development profit divided by total development cost.

hostile.q: You say 16 percent on cost. What happens to that if your rent is wrong?
hostile.a: It is fragile to rent. On these hypothetical numbers, rent 10 percent lower takes profit from about 1.4 million to about 400,000 dollars, around 4.6 percent on cost, because cost does not move. That is why I am testing rent with a market study before we commit, and why I put that risk in the summary rather than the appendix.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The listening room: a landowner, a question behind the question, and silence
summary: In a first meeting with a landowner the person who listens best learns the most, and what you learn decides the deal. This lesson sets a realistic scene, gives the lines to say and never to say, shows how to find the question behind the question, and teaches when to stay silent and how to hold your state.
body:
Mr Shabazz, in a first meeting with a landowner you are not there to present. You are there to find out what the owner actually needs, and you will learn it only if you talk less than they do and say back what you heard.

Recall

Q. What does bottom line up front mean in a meeting?

A. State the answer or the request first, so the listener knows what you want before the reasons begin.

Q. What is the sunk cost trap?

A. Letting money already spent, which cannot be recovered, drive a decision that should be made only on costs and benefits from today forward.

Q. Name three seats at a developer's table besides your own.

A. For example the lender, the landowner and the contractor; others include the architect, the planning authority, the buyer or tenant and the investor.

Why this matters

Land deals are rarely won on price alone. Owners sell for reasons: a family wants to settle an estate, a retiring farmer wants certainty, a business owner wants to keep using the property for a while. The first buyer who understands the real reason can often structure an offer that meets it, sometimes at a lower headline price than a rival who never asked. Bottom line first is how you speak. Listening is how you find out what your bottom line should be.

The scene

A hypothetical. You meet the owner of a two-acre site at the edge of town, at her kitchen table. She inherited it from her father and has had two approaches from other developers this year. She offers coffee, mentions that her father farmed here for forty years, and says, "So, what are you offering?"

The temptation is to answer the question. Resist it. You do not yet know enough to make an offer that wins, and any number you say now becomes the anchor for everything after it, as you learned in Week 3.

Lines to say

Open by setting the purpose, briefly: "Thank you for seeing me. I'd like to make you an offer that works, and I can only do that if I understand what matters to you. Could I ask a few questions first?"

Then ask open questions, which are questions that cannot be answered with yes or no: "What would a good outcome look like for you?" "What did you think of the other approaches?" "How soon would you want this settled?" "Is there anything about the land you would want protected?"

Then summarise back. This is the core of active listening, a practice drawn from the psychologist Carl Rogers' work on counselling and now standard in negotiation training: you restate what you heard in your own words and check it. "So, if I have this right, price matters, but what matters more is that this is settled within a year and that the oak trees along the road are kept. Is that fair?" If she corrects you, you have learned something. If she agrees, she now knows you were listening, which builds the trust you met in Week 3.

Lines never to say

Never say a number in the first meeting unless you have done the work behind it. Never disparage the other developers; she may have liked one of them. Never say "trust me", which tells a cautious seller to do the opposite. Never promise anything you cannot control, such as an approval date, because the planning authority holds that gate, not you. And never say "to be honest", which implies that the rest was not.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: ask, summarise, check, and only then offer.

The question behind the question

Plain English: people often ask one thing when they mean another. "What are you offering?" may really mean "Are you serious, or just another developer fishing?" or "Will you pay more than the last one?" or "Will this be over soon?"

Worked example one. Later the owner asks, "How long would all this take?" A literal answer is a project timeline. But listen to what came before: she mentioned her brother twice, and that the property taxes are a burden. The question behind the question may be, "Can I get out from under this before another year of tax and family argument?" So you answer both: "If we agree terms, the purchase could be conditional on approvals that may take some months. But I could look at a structure where you receive a non-refundable deposit at signing, so part of the money comes sooner." You have not committed to anything. You have shown that you heard the real concern, and you have opened a structure that might be worth more to her than a higher price later.

Worked example two. She says, "The last developer said he would pay 1,000,000 dollars." That is a hypothetical figure. The surface question is "Will you match it?" The question behind it may be, "I did not trust him; do I trust you?" Ask before you react: "What happened with that conversation?" If she says he wanted a long, uncertain conditional period, you have learned that certainty, not price, broke that deal.

When to stay silent

Silence is the most underused tool in a negotiation. After you ask a question, stop talking, even if the pause feels long. Most people fill a silence; the owner will often add the most useful sentence of the meeting a few seconds after her first answer. After she names a figure or a condition, pause before you respond, so your reply is chosen rather than reflexive. The pause also signals that you take her words seriously.

Holding your state is what makes silence possible. If you feel the urge to fill a gap, use the tools from Week 4: a slower exhale, feet on the floor, attention on her words rather than on your next line. Slow breathing is for when you are seated, as here, never while driving. A steady, slower voice reads as confidence; a rushed one reads as need.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving the meeting with an anchor you set too early, or with an obligation you did not mean to create. The control is to end with a clear, non-committal next step: "Thank you. I'd like to put a written proposal to you within two weeks that reflects what you've told me. Nothing is agreed until we both sign something." Then follow up in writing with your summary of what she told you, which gives her the chance to correct it and gives you a record.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a meeting goes well if he spoke well. A first land meeting goes well if the owner spoke more, and you leave knowing her timetable, her real concern, the alternatives she has and what she would need to say yes. If you spoke more than about a third of the time, you probably learned too little. That third is a practitioner habit, not a research finding, but it is a useful check. Afterwards, write down from memory her three main concerns in her words. If you cannot, you were waiting to talk rather than listening, and the next meeting should open by asking again.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught that trust grows from consistent behaviour over time and from showing you understand the other side's interests. The summary-back is trust built in real time: you prove understanding in front of her. The written follow-up is the consistency: you did what you said you would, when you said you would.

Recap

Set the purpose, ask open questions, summarise back and check. Look for the question behind the question, and answer the real concern without committing. Use silence after questions and before replies. Do not set an anchor or make a promise you cannot keep. End with a clear next step, then confirm your understanding in writing.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, with six questions, a Red Pen drill and a two-minute boardroom explanation of the week.
checklist: Write three open questions before any first meeting with a landowner or partner.
State the meeting's purpose in one or two sentences, then ask before you offer.
Summarise back what you heard and check it at least twice in the meeting.
Pause after every question you ask and after every figure they name.
Do not name a price unless you have done the work behind it.
End with a dated next step and the words: nothing is agreed until we both sign.
Send a written summary of what you heard within a day.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a first land meeting I am not there to present. I am there to find out what the owner actually needs. So I set the purpose briefly, then I ask open questions: what would a good outcome look like, how soon do you want this settled, what mattered about the other approaches. Then I summarise back what I heard and check it, which is active listening, and it builds trust in real time. I listen for the question behind the question. How long will this take may really mean can I get out from under the taxes and the family argument this year, and I can answer that with structure, not just price. After I ask a question, I stay silent, because the most useful sentence often comes a few seconds later. I do not set an anchor I have not earned or promise an approval I do not control. I end with a dated next step and confirm in writing.
terms: Active listening — restating in your own words what the other person said and checking it, to confirm understanding and show it.
Open question — a question that cannot be answered with yes or no, used to draw out reasons, priorities and constraints.
The question behind the question — the real concern a person holds that their literal question only partly expresses.

hostile.q: I have had two offers this year. Why should I spend any more time with you?
hostile.a: Because I would rather make you an offer that fits what you need than one that only competes on a number. If you can tell me what a good outcome looks like for you, the timing and anything about the land you want protected, I will put a written proposal to you within two weeks. If it does not fit, you will have lost one coffee.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 5 review: bottom line first, listening and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions on the week's ideas, a one-page recap, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical lender email with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of why clear communication is a money and risk control.
body:
This week's single idea: the answer goes first, the risk goes in plain words, and you listen more than you speak, because unclear messages cost time, money and sometimes far more. Today you test it, mark up a bad email and say the week aloud in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What two costs does a delayed decision create on a funded project?

A. Carrying cost, which reduces profit, and time, because the reduced profit arrives later and so the annual return falls further.

Q. Name two of Cialdini's principles of influence.

A. For example reciprocity and social proof; the others include commitment and consistency, authority, liking and scarcity.

Q. What is Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, communication is the medium every other skill in this course travels through. A sound pro forma presented badly loses to a weaker one presented well, and a clear warning written badly can be read as reassurance. Answer each question below aloud before you read the answer, mark any you hesitated on, and reread only that day's lesson. Then try the six again in a week, without looking. Retrieval practised after a gap sticks better than rereading, and the discomfort of the gap is part of how it works.

The six questions

Question 1: What does bottom line up front require?

Answer: The first line of a message states the conclusion, request or decision required, so the reader can stop after one line and still act correctly.

Question 2: What are the three levels of the pyramid principle?

Answer: One answer on top, a few supporting reasons beneath it that do not overlap and together cover the case, and evidence beneath each reason.

Question 3: What is Rule 5?

Answer: When a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out; I never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question.

Question 4: A project has drawn 6,000,000 dollars at 8 percent a year plus 5,000 dollars a week of fixed overhead. What is the weekly carrying cost?

Answer: Interest is 480,000 dollars a year, about 9,230 a week, plus 5,000, so about 14,230 dollars a week.

Question 5: Why can a short email reply bind you?

Answer: Courts in many systems judge agreement objectively, by what a reasonable reader would conclude, so a reply that reads as acceptance can be treated as one, depending on the contract and the law.

Question 6: In a first land meeting, what do you do after asking a question?

Answer: Stay silent and let the owner answer fully, then summarise back what you heard and check it before offering anything.

The week in one page

Day 1 set the structure: bottom line up front, the pyramid of one answer, about three reasons and evidence on request, a pause after the answer, and the correction that the 93 percent non-verbal figure was never about understanding arguments. Day 2, Ford took the loss of Columbia through seven steps: a debris tool used outside its range, a reassuring headline above a warning in small type, stalled requests for images, and a known anomaly that had come to feel normal. Day 3, JAX priced delay as carrying cost and showed the six-line ask that gets a yes in one round. Day 4, LEX explained how replies can bind, what subject to contract and without prejudice are meant to do, and why notices must follow the clause. Day 5, Sage built a bottom line forward from rent to profit, tested rent and the cap rate, and fitted the summary to a two-minute slot. Day 6 put you at a landowner's table: ask, summarise, check, stay silent and only then offer.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical email from a developer to a lender's relationship manager. Read it twice and mark every defect before reading on.

Hi, just following up on last week. As you know we had the site meeting on Tuesday and the engineer looked at the test pits, and we've been talking to the contractor about sequencing and a few other things. Overall things look good and the schedule is generally on track. The geotech mentioned some soft ground in a couple of spots but appears adequate. We may possibly want to think about a short extension at some point, maybe three or four weeks, not sure yet. Also the contractor asked about the extra excavation at 85,000 dollars and I said fine. Let me know your thoughts. Projected value is 9,880,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Say each defect aloud as you find it, then compare.

The defects. First, there is no bottom line: the request, if there is one, is the extension, and it is buried in the fifth sentence. Second, the request is hedged until it means nothing: "may possibly want to think about", "at some point", "not sure yet". A lender cannot approve that, so it will come back as questions, costing weeks of carry. Third, it opens with chronology, the site meeting and the test pits, rather than the answer. Fourth, it breaks Rule 5: "things look good" and "generally on track" sit above "soft ground in a couple of spots", and "appears adequate" is a hedge being read as reassurance. The open risk needs the first line and a statement of what would close it. Fifth, "I said fine" to 85,000 dollars of extra excavation is a casual yes that may have agreed a price and a scope change, without checking whether the work was already in the original scope. Sixth, there is no date for any decision and no consequence of waiting. Seventh, the value figure is unrounded, unexplained and unsourced, with no mention of the assumptions it rests on.

The rewrite opens: "Request: approve a 3-week extension at no change to the loan amount, by Friday. Open risk: two of six boreholes found soft clay; four more boreholes, about two weeks, will confirm the foundation design. I have told the contractor not to start the extra excavation until we confirm whether it is in the original scope."

The boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes and explain this week to an imagined board. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Clear communication is a cost and risk control on our projects, not a style choice. Every request we send opens with the answer and a date, because a vague request comes back as questions, and each round costs us about a week of carrying cost. Every report puts open risks in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to close them, because the loss of Columbia shows how a warning buried under a reassuring headline gets missed. We treat our own emails as potential commitments: we say when we are not agreeing, and formal notices follow the contract's clause. And in negotiations we listen first. We ask, summarise and check before we offer, because what the other side needs decides the structure that wins."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is agreeing with all of it and changing nothing. The control is one template: open your next five emails with a one-sentence bottom line and a date, and put any risk in the first line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks communication skill means sounding impressive. It means the listener can act correctly after one sentence and repeat your point accurately to someone else.

Callback

In Week 2 you built the after-action review: what was meant to happen, what happened, why, and what next. Run it on one message this week that took more than one round to get approved. The question that came back is the line your template was missing.

Recap

Answer first, three reasons, evidence on request. Risks in the first line, with what closes them. Requests with dates and consequences. Replies written as the commitments they may be. Listen more than you talk.

checklist: Question 1: What does bottom line up front require? Answer: The first line of a message states the conclusion, request or decision required, so the reader can stop after one line and still act correctly.

Question 2: What are the three levels of the pyramid principle? Answer: One answer on top, a few supporting reasons beneath it that do not overlap and together cover the case, and evidence beneath each reason.

Question 3: What is Rule 5? Answer: When a message carries a risk, the risk goes in the first line in plain words, with what it would take to rule it out; I never let a reassuring headline sit on top of an open question.

Question 4: A project has drawn 6,000,000 dollars at 8 percent a year plus 5,000 dollars a week of fixed overhead. What is the weekly carrying cost? Answer: Interest is 480,000 dollars a year, about 9,230 a week, plus 5,000, so about 14,230 dollars a week.

Question 5: Why can a short email reply bind you? Answer: Courts in many systems judge agreement objectively, by what a reasonable reader would conclude, so a reply that reads as acceptance can be treated as one, depending on the contract and the law.

Question 6: In a first land meeting, what do you do after asking a question? Answer: Stay silent and let the owner answer fully, then summarise back what you heard and check it before offering anything.
head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned that clear communication is a cost and risk control. I put the bottom line first: the answer or the request, with a date, so the reader can act on one line. Beneath it I give about three reasons that do not overlap, and I keep the evidence for whoever challenges a reason. Rule 5 says any risk goes in the first line in plain words with what it would take to close it, because Columbia showed how a warning beneath a reassuring headline gets missed. A vague request comes back as questions, and each round costs about a week of carrying cost, so I write to answer the committee's questions before they are asked. I treat my replies as possible commitments, and I send notices the way the contract requires. In a negotiation I listen first: I ask, summarise back, stay silent, and only then offer.
terms: Retrieval practice — recalling information from memory before checking it, which strengthens memory more than rereading.
Red Pen drill — marking up a short document with planted defects to train the eye to catch them in real work.
Spaced repetition — reviewing material again after a gap rather than straight away, which improves long-term recall.

hostile.q: Your email said things look good. Why are you now telling me the foundation is an open risk?
hostile.a: Because my email put the reassurance above the risk, and that was wrong. Two of six boreholes found soft clay and the extent is not yet known. Four more boreholes will close it in about two weeks, and I will report the result in the first line of my next update, whatever it shows.
